newsitem.title: USA: Storm hurts North Carolina agriculture - official.
newsitem.headline: Storm hurts North Carolina agriculture - official.

text.p: Hurricane Fran, which slammed into North Carolina last week, affected every farm in its path and may have caused billions of dollars of damage to farming operations, a North Carolina agriculture official said.
"We are talking about a storm that was 150 miles wide," North Carolina Department of Agriculture public affairs director Jim Knight told Reuters in a telephone interview.
"No major (agricultural) structures were damaged but we are seeing impact on virtually every farm that was in the path of the storm," he said.

The damage from Fran is expected to eclipse losses incurred by Hurricane Hugo and Hurricane Hazel which hammered the state in 1989 and in 1954, respectively. "We are easily into the billions (of dollars) and in Wake County alone, damage will surpass the one billion dollar mark," Knight said.
The Federal Emergency Management Agency and Farm Service agency personnel are presently evaluating agricultural damage.

"It will be at least a week before we will know the extent of damage and how quickly it will take to affect both short and long-term repairs not only in agriculture but the entire infrastructure of the state," Knight said.
On North Carolina's poultry and hog industry, Knight cited death losses but the extent was not known due to damaged communication lines and power outages.
"We know there has been death loss in the poultry and and in swine industry from North Carolina/South Carolina border up through Wake County to the Virgina line," Knight said.
North Carolina ranks second in the nation, behind Iowa, in pork production because it holds many large, corporate farms.

These farms which suffered from power outages last week rely on electricity. Many of these hog and poultry farms use their own well water not only for drinking purposes but for cooling their livestock.

"If there is no electricity, they can not pump water," he said. A lot of rural customers get supply from electrical coops and Knight said there was no way of knowing how many of these coops are back up and running.
Even the state's corn crop, already significantly damaged by Hurricane Bertha this July, was effected. Any of the corn that was in the path of the storm was either damaged or destroyed," Knight said.

Also, "we have heard early reports of farmers reporting complete loss of their cotton crop to others who had what appeared to be minor damage, depending on the stage of maturity and degree of the boll opening," he said.
"We had about 800,000 acres of planted cotton this year and we have no idea how many acres we will be able to harvest," Knight said.
Based on the August crop production report, North Carolina ranked seventh this year among U.S. cotton producing states with an estimated 1.04 million bales.
Even the state's tobacco crop had major problems.

"First was immediate wind damage to the plant still in the field and secondly, to the tobacco that was in the curing barns when they (producers) loss electricity," Knight said. "If there is no air circulating through the tobacco in the curing barns, the tobacco will sour and eventually rot," he said.
